title: Two dots or three: the range syntax that decides your release notes
summary: A..B and A...B mean different things for log and yet another thing for diff. Get them wrong and your changelog silently omits half the work.
mental_model: For log: `A..B` is 'in B, not in A'. `A...B` is the symmetric difference — in either, not both. For diff it is reversed in spirit: `A..B` compares endpoints, `A...B` compares B against the merge base. Log and diff genuinely disagree, which is the trap.

steps.title: See the fork you are about to describe
steps.why: main and feature/dosing both moved after v1.0. Every range question below is really 'which side of this fork do I mean'.

steps.title: Two dots: what is on the branch and not on main
steps.why: `main..feature/dosing` reads as 'commits reachable from feature/dosing but not from main'. This is the correct range for 'what would this pull request add'.
steps.expect: Two commits — only the branch's own work.

verify.label: two-dot range isolates the branch's commits

steps.title: Reverse it to find what you are missing
steps.why: Flipping the operands answers the other question: what has main gained that the branch has not seen? This is the range that tells you whether you need to rebase.

steps.title: Three dots: everything on either side
steps.why: `A...B` is the symmetric difference. With `--left-right`, `<` marks commits on the left side and `>` on the right — the clearest picture of a divergence you can get in one command.

steps.title: Now the trap: diff means the opposite thing
steps.why: `git diff main..feature/dosing` compares the two tips, so it includes main's changes as removals. `git diff main...feature/dosing` compares against the merge base — the branch's work alone. Code review tools use three dots; people typing by hand usually use two, and get a diff full of unrelated deletions.
steps.expect: Two dots mentions security.py and app.py. Three dots mentions only dosing.py.

steps.title: Exclusion syntax, for more than two branches
steps.why: `^main` means 'not reachable from main' and composes with any number of refs. `A..B` is just shorthand for `^A B`.

steps.title: Write the release notes
steps.why: Everything since the last tag, no merges, one line each. This is a real changelog command, and it is the two-dot form because you want commits, not a diff.

verify.label: the changelog range covers exactly the two post-tag commits
you can name just the branch's commits
three-dot diff shows only what the branch changed
verify.hint: this is the diff a pull request displays

verify.label: two-dot diff also drags in main's own changes — the trap

pitfalls: log and diff use the dots oppositely. If a range surprises you, ask which of the two commands you are running.
`git diff A..B` in a pull-request context shows deletions that nobody made — they are just changes on the base branch.
Ranges need both refs to exist locally. `origin/main..main` is only accurate after a fetch.
`--left-right` without `--oneline` is hard to read. The two flags belong together.
cheatsheet: commits in B that are not in A
both sides of a divergence, marked
the same as A..B, composable with more refs
what B changed since it forked — the PR diff
